finding.reasoning:
This is a real defect in the shipped app. The system prompt asks the model to express thresholds in canonical units, and the schema makes it report a `unit` for every item. When the model keeps the protocol's own unit (for example "Hb ≥ 100 g/L", which is common in EU and Canadian protocols, "ANC ≥ 1500/µL", or "HbA1c ≥ 53 mmol/mol"), the app takes the number as written and silently runs it against observations that were converted to the canonical unit. The error is a factor of 10, 1000 or a different scale entirely, which turns a lab inclusion into an almost universal fail, or an exclusion into a no-op. There is no warning or chip. For a feasibility tool this quietly distorts the eligible pool and the enrollment forecasts that feed site and country decisions. A reviewer would only catch it by reading every AI rule's number.

The rule-based parser already converts units (UNIT_CONV and normalizeUnits, which set unitNote), and the observation side converts through UNIT_RULES/convertObs, so the AI path is the odd one out. Severity is medium rather than high for three reasons: the error needs the model to disobey the canonical-unit instruction, the rules are shown for human review before use, and AI interpretation is an optional assist. It is still a silent wrong answer when it happens.

The fix reuses convertObs, the same table that converts patient observations, so thresholds and observations are guaranteed to land in the same unit. Units it cannot convert are not guessed: the rule becomes manual/unresolved with an invalidReason, the same way validateCriterion failures are handled. A null unit or the canonical unit (whitespace and case-insensitive, with 10⁹ and 10³ superscripts normalised) keeps today's behaviour. So does a "× ULN" unit when uln_multiple is set, because the value is then the canonical multiple × ULN. validateLlmItem also gains a type check on `unit` (string or null), matching its other per-field checks.

In fhirToRaw's Observation branch (around line 1645) the only check is that valueQuantity holds a finite number. Observation.status is never read.
The Condition branch right above it already drops verificationStatus refuted and entered-in-error, and the medication branch maps status to active. So the Observation branch is the odd one out, not a deliberate design choice.
In FHIR R4, entered-in-error means the result was withdrawn and should not have existed. Cancelled means the test was not done. Neither may drive eligibility.
Because buildClinical takes the most recent observation per lab, a retracted result does more than add noise. It overrides the valid earlier result. In the real browser this flipped a patient from 'fails' (HbA1c 9.0) to 'meets' (6.5).
That inflates the eligible-patient counts that site selection and enrolment forecasts rest on. Nothing warns the user: the observation shows as accepted.
Policy for non-final results:
- preliminary and registered: still used, which is reasonable for pre-screening feasibility, but counted and shown in the import report.

finding.reasoning:
The finding is correct. When parseComparison() sees a lower bound followed by an upper bound (">/>= X ... </<= Y"), it merges them into {op:'between', min, max} and drops which operators were used. cmpNum's 'between' always tests v >= min && v <= max.

Every strict range is therefore evaluated as inclusive. That affects:
- age: the parser keeps all comparison fields through `...c` (spread), so the strictness is lost there too;
- labs: line ~2223 copies only min and max;
- lines of therapy and biomarkers: also spread.

The Logic column (critLogic) prints BETWEEN, which reads as inclusive, so a reviewer checking the rule against the protocol cannot see the error. The PARSER_TESTS BMI case (">17 and <35" expected as "BMI BETWEEN 17 AND 35") enshrines the bug.

Why it matters in a clinical-trial feasibility tool: patients exactly at a boundary are counted as eligible (or, for exclusions, excluded) when they should not be. Integer ages ("> 18 and < 65") and lab or score values recorded at round thresholds are common, so cohort counts and site estimates are skewed. Fully strict wording is less common than ≥/≤ in protocols but does occur, and half-open ranges ("≥ 18 and < 65") are frequent. The error is systematic rather than random noise, and it is invisible in the generated logic text. It is not high severity because only boundary values are affected and these are cohort estimates, not patient-level enrollment decisions.

There is no Monte Carlo kernel involvement: src/ has no criterion evaluation.

The '(v0.9.4 defaults)' tag keeps them honest in v0.9.5, whose changelog adds benchmark import without changing the default engine. The figures also do not describe runs where the user has applied overrides or benchmarks, and the wording only claims them for the defaults.

In the bid summary and the site pack, 'not validated predictions' is followed by 'Not independently validated', which is slightly repetitive. The repetition is deliberate: it keeps the constant self-contained for the manifest JSON.

Other 'unvalidated model' phrases elsewhere in the UI and reports stay as they are. They are defensible but could be harmonised in a later pass.
